overview.intro: Political science is the study of power, government and the arrangements by which people live together in organised communities. This unit establishes the vocabulary the rest of the course uses: what political science studies and how its branches relate, what makes a State a State through its four elements, and why a State is not the same thing as a Nation even though the two words are used interchangeably in everyday speech.

learningOutcomes: Explain the meaning and scope of political science and its main branches.
Describe the four elements of the State.
Distinguish the State from government, society and nation.
Explain why sovereignty is the defining element of the State.
Apply the concepts to contemporary political situations.

learn.title: Meaning and scope of political science

blocks.text: Political science is the systematic study of the political: the ways in which power is acquired, exercised and contested, the institutions through which collective decisions are made, and the ideas that justify or challenge those institutions. Aristotle called man a political animal because he argued that human beings can only fulfil themselves within a polis, and though later thinkers disputed that conclusion, the subject has remained centred on the question of how strangers are to live together under authority. It is a social science in that it uses evidence and comparison, and a humanity in that its central questions — justice, liberty, obligation — cannot be settled by measurement alone.

items: Political science studies power in both its coercive and its consensual forms.
Its method combines institutional description, comparison and normative argument.
It overlaps with economics, sociology, history and law without being reducible to any of them.
Its practical use is in judging institutions rather than merely describing them.

learn.title: The four elements of the State

blocks.text: A State exists only where four elements are present together. Population means a human community of a size that permits social life; the number itself is irrelevant, since the smallest republic and the largest federation are equally States. Territory means a defined area over which the State’s authority runs, including land, waters and airspace; a wandering people without settled territory may form a nation but not a State. Government is the machinery through which the State’s will is formulated and carried out, including the legislature, the executive and the courts, together with the officials who administer policy.

Sovereignty is the fourth and decisive element: the supreme, independent and enduring authority within a territory, which acknowledges no superior in law. Internal sovereignty means that the State’s commands bind everyone within its borders, and external sovereignty means that it is not subject to another power in international law. Remove any element and the State disappears: a population scattered across the globe, a territory without authority, a government that obeys an external master in all things — each fails the test. The elements are therefore not a list of desirable features but the conditions without which the word State has no meaning.

items.text: The United Nations has population, territory and a secretariat but no sovereignty.
items.note: It is an organisation of States, not a State, because its authority derives from member consent.

items.text: A government-in-exile retains its claim but not its territory.
items.note: It shows that territory is an element of the State and not merely of its government.

learn.title: State, government, society and nation distinguished

blocks.text: The State is the largest and most formal of these ideas: a population, a territory and a government bound together by sovereignty. Government is only the instrument of the State, a subset of its institutions that makes and enforces decisions; governments change constantly while the State continues. Society is wider still in one direction and narrower in another: it includes families, firms, clubs and faith communities that exist alongside the State and often predate it, but it lacks sovereignty and does not claim a monopoly of legitimate force within a territory.

The Nation is a different kind of thing altogether. It is a community of people who believe they belong together, usually through a common language, history, culture or descent — what writers on nationalism call a shared identity recognised by its members. A Nation may exist without a State, as peoples have done for centuries; a State may contain several Nations, as multinational states regularly do; and a State may be built where the Nation is itself an argument, as the history of many border redrawings shows. The State is therefore defined by law and authority, the Nation by identity and mutual recognition.

Voluntary and inherited ties without sovereignty
Do the people think of themselves as one?

learn.title: Why the concepts matter, and how they are criticised

blocks.text: These distinctions are the working tools of the subject. Calling a body a State when it has no sovereignty leads to confused claims about recognition and membership; treating government as the State hides the continuity of institutions behind the change of ministers; and assuming that every Nation must have its own State turns every minority into a potential secession. Examiners reward answers that keep the terms apart under pressure, because most errors in political writing come from sliding between them.

Critics raise two objections worth knowing. The first is that the four-element definition fits the modern territorial state so well that it struggles with city-states of the past, empires and supranational unions. The second is that sovereignty itself, the element that carries the definition, is hard to locate once states join organisations that bind them in law: a member of a union that can legislate directly is still sovereign in law while no longer free in practice. The response is that the elements define the State as an analytical concept, and that cases which stretch it tell us where the concept needs care rather than that it fails.

items: Concepts are what allow an answer to be marked rather than merely read.
The four-element test is quick and reliable for borderline cases.
Sovereignty is where the definition does its real work.
Stretch cases — unions, empires, exiles — test the concept without destroying it.

keyPoints: Political science studies power, institutions and the ideas that justify them.
Its branches include theory, comparative politics, administration, international relations and law.
The four elements of the State are population, territory, government and sovereignty.
Sovereignty is supreme, independent authority and is the decisive test of a State.
Internal sovereignty binds everyone inside the territory; external sovereignty answers to no superior in law.
Government is the instrument of the State and changes while the State continues.
Society includes associations that lack sovereignty and a monopoly of force.
The Nation is a community of shared identity and may exist without a State.
A single State may contain several Nations or be formed where Nation and State do not coincide.
Conceptual confusion, not difficulty of material, is the commonest cause of lost marks.
examFocus: A State question must walk through all four elements with the consequence of removing each.
Distinction questions are best answered as a table on one basis at a time.
Sovereignty carries the definition; an answer that omits it does not identify a State.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four elements of the State?
questions.explanation: The four elements are population, territory, government and sovereignty; public opinion influences the State but does not constitute it.

questions.prompt: The element that distinguishes the State from an association such as the United Nations is:
questions.explanation: The United Nations has population and territory but its authority derives from its members, so it lacks sovereignty.

questions.prompt: A people with a common language, history and culture but no territory of their own would be called a:
questions.explanation: The Nation is defined by shared identity and mutual recognition, which may exist without the legal structure of a State.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes State from government?
options: They are the same thing under different names
The State is the enduring sovereign entity; government is its changing administrative machinery
The State is smaller than government
Government is permanent and the State changes
questions.answer: The State is the enduring sovereign entity; government is its changing administrative machinery
questions.explanation: Governments come and go through election and succession while the State continues as the sovereign person in law.

questions.prompt: The branch of political science that studies concepts such as justice, liberty and the State is political __________ .
questions.explanation: Political theory examines the ideas through which political institutions are justified or criticised.

questions.prompt: The branch of political science that compares different political systems by institution and performance is __________ politics.
questions.explanation: Comparative politics sets political systems beside one another so that differences in institution and outcome can be explained rather than merely described.

questions.prompt: State the four elements of the State and explain the importance of any two.
questions.answer: The four elements are population, territory, government and sovereignty. Territory matters because authority must run somewhere: without defined land, water and airspace there is no area within which commands bind, which is why a government-in-exile exercises no effective authority. Sovereignty matters most because it is the test that separates a State from every other body: it makes the State’s law supreme inside its borders and its person equal with other States outside them. Population and government are equally required — a community to govern and a machinery to act for it — but answers normally earn the most on sovereignty.
questions.explanation: All four elements must be named, and two must be explained as conditions rather than described.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the State and the Nation.
questions.answer: The State is a legal and political entity defined by four elements, of which sovereignty is decisive; it commands, legislates and claims a monopoly of legitimate force over a defined territory. The Nation is a community defined by identity — a shared language, history, culture or descent — and by the recognition its members give one another; it legislates nothing and claims no monopoly of force. The two can therefore come apart in either direction: a Nation may live for centuries without a State of its own, as peoples without territory have done, and a single State may contain several Nations within its borders, which is why multinational states exist. Conversely a State may be constructed where national identity is still contested. The State is thus a question of authority, the Nation a question of belonging.
questions.explanation: Three points of contrast plus the two ways the concepts come apart earn full marks.

questions.prompt: Examine the four elements of the State and explain why sovereignty is the most important of them.
questions.answer: A State requires population, territory, government and sovereignty together, and the first three supply the material conditions of political life. Population provides the human community whose members are bound by the State’s laws, and its size is immaterial, since the smallest republic and the largest federation are equally States. Territory provides the area over which authority runs, including land, water and airspace, and without boundaries there is nothing to distinguish one jurisdiction from another. Government provides the machinery — legislature, executive, courts and the administrative services — through which the will of the State is formulated and carried out, and it is this element that changes with elections while the State continues. Sovereignty is nevertheless the most important, for two reasons. First, it is definitional: population, territory and government are found in companies, cities and international organisations, but only the State claims supreme legal authority within its territory and equal standing outside it, so a body without sovereignty is not a State in any sense. Second, it is functional: only because its law is supreme can the State settle disputes finally, tax, and enforce a common order, whereas a government subject to an external master in all things is an administration, not a sovereign authority. Cases such as members of supranational unions show that sovereignty can be qualified in practice, but they do not remove the test, because the question of where final legal authority lies still has an answer.
questions.explanation: Full marks need all four elements described and a two-part justification for sovereignty: definitional and functional.

questions.prompt: A federation such as India has governments at two levels, each with its own powers. Discuss whether sovereignty is divided in such a system.
questions.answer: The appearance of divided sovereignty comes from the fact that federal constitutions distribute legislative power: Parliament and the state legislatures each have subjects on which they may make law, and each has its own institutions and revenue. The classical answer, associated with dual federalism, was that this was a division of functions rather than of sovereignty, because the constitution itself remained the supreme law and the union retained the authority to amend it, to legislate on residuary subjects and to intervene in defined circumstances. On this reading sovereignty is like a lamp that lends its light to several rooms without being split. The opposing argument is stronger in practice than it looks: if a constituent unit can block constitutional change, control its own police and administration in substance, and resist enforcement, then the centre’s supremacy exists on paper only, and sovereignty has in fact been shared. The answer turns on where final authority actually lies in the last resort — in the courts, in the amending power, or in the capacity to enforce — rather than on how many subjects each legislature enjoys. Most constitutions keep the formal answer indivisible while allowing practical power to be deeply shared, and a strong essay shows that the two questions, where sovereign authority lies and how power is exercised, are not identical.
questions.explanation: The best answers separate formal legal sovereignty from practical political power and reach a reasoned judgement about the last resort.
